headline: A rough night on Wall Street — NASDAQ tanked 4.2% — is dragging on your tech holdings, while PLS.AX had its worst day of the week dropping 3.75% on continued lithium weakness.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: Pilbara had a tough session today, falling 3.75% to $5.91. Lithium and gold stocks broadly slid across the ASX mining sector, and sentiment on PLS remains divided — some investors see value, others are waiting for a clearer bottom. You're now sitting 12.3% below your entry price on this one.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft dropped 2.66% last night to $416.67, its biggest single-session fall in the portfolio. The NASDAQ sold off hard (down 4.18%), dragging big tech names with it. Despite Microsoft's strong AI story coming out of Build 2026, the broader market mood turned risk-off (investors pulling money out of growth stocks) last night.

movers.name: Global X AI ETF
movers.note: GXAI.AX fell 1.74% today to $18.05, reflecting weakness in AI-linked tech stocks globally. The ETF tracks AI companies heavily exposed to NASDAQ, which had a horror session last night. Still getting positive analyst coverage locally though — Motley Fool flagged it as one of the top ASX ETFs for the AI decade.

movers.name: Vanguard Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE.AX dipped 0.94% today to $92.03. Emerging markets copped a hit partly from the weaker Australian dollar (down 1.16% against the USD), which reduces the AUD value of international holdings when the Aussie falls.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: Take-Two slipped 1.04% last night to $214.39, dragged along by the broad NASDAQ selloff. No company-specific news; just caught in the wider tech downdraft. Still sitting 7.5% below your entry cost overall.

movers.name: Alphabet Inc. (Google)
movers.note: Google fell 0.95% last night to $365.76 — a relatively modest drop compared to the broader NASDAQ carnage (down 4.18%). It's actually your best-performing US holding, up 26.5% from your entry price. The stock held up reasonably well despite general tech selling.

movers.name: BetaShares Global Energy ETF
movers.note: FUEL.AX nudged down 0.8% today to $8.70. Oil (WTI crude) dropped 2.69% last night to $90.54 a barrel after Goldman Sachs flagged a big hit to global oil demand and trimmed their price forecasts. Energy stocks typically follow the oil price, so this drag makes sense.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market ETF
movers.note: VTS.AX edged up 0.31% today to $521.82 — a small positive despite the wild NASDAQ session last night. The ETF tracks the broader US market (not just tech), so it's more insulated from pure tech selloffs. A small but welcome move in the right direction.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG.AX barely moved today, up a modest 0.12% to $75.95. Its diversified mix of global shares and bonds provided some cushioning on a day when tech stocks were under pressure. This one's doing its job as a steady long-term compounder.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX — Hold, but keep watching lithium sentiment
watch_today.detail: Pilbara dropped 3.75% today and is now 12.3% below your entry. The stock remains a battleground — Goldman Sachs flagged global demand risks and the broader mining sector is under pressure. No clear catalyst to buy more yet, but no company-specific crisis either. Hold and watch.

watch_today.title: MSFT — Hold despite last night's 2.66% drop
watch_today.detail: Microsoft was smacked last night alongside the NASDAQ's 4.18% plunge. That said, the Microsoft Build 2026 event this week was packed with AI announcements that analysts are still processing. The business fundamentals remain strong — this looks like market noise rather than a Microsoft-specific problem. Hold.

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX — Hold with a positive longer-term outlook
watch_today.detail: Down 1.74% today, but local analysts (Motley Fool, Kalkine) are still bullish on AI ETFs for the decade ahead. Trump's new AI executive order and growing regulation globally are shaping the sector — worth watching how that evolves. No reason to sell, and the dip could be a longer-term entry opportunity if you have dry powder.

watch_today.title: NASDAQ tanked 4.18% last night — US markets open again tonight
watch_today.detail: The NASDAQ fell over 1,100 points last night — a big risk-off move (investors fleeing growth stocks). Your GOOGL, MSFT, and TTWO are all exposed. Watch tonight's US open (~11:30 PM AEST) to see if the selloff continues or stabilises. If it extends, GXAI.AX and VTS.AX will likely feel more pain tomorrow.

watch_today.title: RBA rate cut expectations building — good for VDHG, property
watch_today.detail: CBA is now forecasting the RBA (Reserve Bank of Australia) will cut interest rates. Lower rates are generally good for share markets and growth assets like VDHG. The RBA deputy also defended past rate hikes this week, but the market is increasingly betting on cuts ahead — a tailwind for your diversified holdings.

watch_today.title: Oil dropping — headwind for FUEL.AX this week
watch_today.detail: WTI crude oil fell 2.69% last night to $90.54 after Goldman Sachs downgraded its global oil demand outlook. FUEL.AX tracks global energy companies, which follow the oil price closely. Keep an eye on whether oil stabilises or keeps sliding — another leg down would hurt FUEL.AX further.

markets.summary: Last night on Wall Street was ugly — the NASDAQ lost 4.18% and the S&P 500 dropped 2.64%, with big tech leading the selloff. Gold fell 3.1% and oil dropped 2.69%, suggesting investors moved into a broadly risk-off (sell-everything) mood. Closer to home, the ASX 200 closed down a relatively mild 0.7% today, cushioned by its heavier weighting towards banks and resources. The Aussie dollar slipped 1.16% to 70.5 US cents.

indicators.name: ASX 200
indicators.note: Modest fall today — banks and miners provided some buffer against global tech weakness.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Last night's session — broad selloff led by tech. Risk-off mood across the board.

indicators.name: NASDAQ
indicators.note: Last night — worst of the major indices. Over 1,100 points lost in a single session.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Last night — Goldman Sachs cut demand forecasts, knocking the oil price sharply.

indicators.name: Gold
indicators.note: Last night — unusual for gold to fall in a risk-off move; suggests some forced selling.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: Aussie dollar weakened — makes your US holdings worth a little less in AUD terms.

politics.summary: The big domestic story is the RBA and interest rates — multiple angles today on where rates are headed, with CBA forecasting cuts and the RBA's own deputy defending the hike cycle. Labor's new tax proposals are also stirring debate, with changes to capital gains tax and trust rules potentially hitting investors and charities.

stories.title: CBA forecasts RBA interest rate cuts ahead
stories.why_it_matters: Australia's biggest bank, CBA, is now officially forecasting that the Reserve Bank will cut interest rates. This is a meaningful shift — when CBA calls it, markets take notice. Rate cuts are generally good news for share markets (cheaper borrowing = more investment) and would ease mortgage pressure for homeowners. No specific timeline was published in the available data, but the direction of travel is now clearly toward lower rates.

stories.title: Labor's 30% tax on capital gains and trusts deals a blow to charities
stories.why_it_matters: Labor is pushing a 30% tax on capital gains (profits from selling investments) and income distributed through trusts. Currently, individuals get a 50% discount on capital gains tax (CGT) when they sell an asset held over 12 months — Labor's changes would effectively increase the tax hit. The AFR reports this is also hitting charities that use trusts to manage their finances. If you hold investments in a trust structure, this is worth watching closely.

stories.title: Treasurer defends $53 billion debt burden
stories.why_it_matters: Treasurer Jim Chalmers faced questions this week over the government's $53 billion debt position, responding it's 'not a lot' in the context of the overall economy. Critics disagree. High government spending is one of the factors the RBA has flagged as putting upward pressure on inflation and interest rates — so this debate has real implications for how quickly rates can come down.

stories.title: RBA pressed on government spending's impact on interest rates
stories.why_it_matters: The RBA was grilled this week on whether the federal government's big spending is making it harder to cut interest rates. The Reserve Bank has previously noted that government spending adds to demand in the economy, which can fuel inflation — the very thing rate hikes are meant to fight. It's a tension between fiscal policy (what the government spends) and monetary policy (what the RBA does with rates), and it's not going away anytime soon.

ai.summary: AI regulation is dominating the headlines globally — Trump signed a new executive order that could change how companies like Google and OpenAI roll out models, while a US federal bill is freezing state-level consumer protections. Separately, the top AI CEOs are making an unusual joint push to Congress on biosecurity. Microsoft's Build 2026 conference wrapped with a big AI announcement dump.

stories.title: Trump's new AI order could change how OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic launch models
stories.why_it_matters: Trump signed an executive order that would give the federal government more say over how AI companies like OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic release new AI models. The order appears designed to make sure the US government has visibility — and potentially veto power — over major AI launches, framing AI as too strategically important to leave entirely to private companies. For Google (GOOGL) and Microsoft (MSFT), this adds a layer of regulatory risk to their AI product roadmaps.

stories.title: Federal AI Regulation Bill freezes state consumer protections for three years
stories.why_it_matters: A federal AI bill in the US would override individual state laws protecting consumers from AI harms — for three years. States like California that had pushed ahead with their own AI rules are now facing a freeze on those protections. Critics call it a giveaway to big tech companies, allowing them to operate without state-level oversight while a federal framework slowly takes shape. This is sparking significant political backlash across the US.

stories.title: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Microsoft CEOs urge Congress to mandate synthetic DNA screening
stories.why_it_matters: In an unusual move, the CEOs of OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Microsoft jointly wrote to Congress asking for laws requiring DNA synthesis companies to screen orders for dangerous pathogens. The concern is that AI tools are now powerful enough to help bad actors design biological threats — and DNA synthesis (essentially printing custom DNA sequences) is becoming easier and cheaper. It's a rare moment of the tech industry proactively asking for regulation, and signals just how seriously these companies view AI-enabled biosecurity risks.

stories.title: Microsoft Build 2026: 7 Biggest AI Announcements You Need to Know
stories.why_it_matters: Microsoft's annual developer conference, Build 2026, wrapped up this week with a string of major AI product announcements. The article highlights 7 key reveals — though the full article text wasn't available, Build conferences typically feature new Copilot (Microsoft's AI assistant) capabilities, Azure AI cloud updates, and developer tools. These announcements reinforce Microsoft's position as a leading AI platform provider, which is central to the bull case for MSFT despite last night's share price drop.

stories.title: UN calls for AI regulation amid expanding environmental footprint
stories.why_it_matters: The United Nations is ramping up calls for global AI regulation, pointing to the growing environmental cost of running large AI systems. Data centres powering AI models consume enormous amounts of electricity and water — this is becoming a political issue as much as a technical one. For investors in AI-exposed ETFs like GXAI.AX, regulatory and environmental compliance costs are a long-term factor worth keeping in mind.

sport.summary: Big NRL weekend — the Titans pulled off a stunning upset over the Broncos at Suncorp, the Dolphins demolished the Cowboys, and the Roosters crushed the Raiders. In AFL, Fremantle handed North Melbourne their biggest-ever loss under Chris Clarkson. French Open semifinal action also continues in Paris.

stories.title: Titans stun Broncos 28-23 in 'Suncorp miracle' finish
stories.why_it_matters: The Gold Coast Titans beat the Brisbane Broncos 28-23 in what Fox Sports is calling an 'all-time try' moment at Suncorp Stadium tonight. The Broncos led but couldn't hold on — it's been described as a 'miracle' finish and continues a miserable stretch of form for Brisbane. For Gold Coast fans, a win over the Broncos at their home ground is about as good as it gets.

stories.title: Dolphins thrash Cowboys 40-14 — Origin stars shine
stories.why_it_matters: The Dolphins put on a masterclass against the Cowboys in North Queensland today, winning 40-14 — extending what Fox Sports calls their 'picket fence' (unbeaten run). State of Origin representatives starred for the Dolphins in a dominant team performance. The Cowboys were well beaten at home, which will hurt their top-8 aspirations.

stories.title: Roosters dismantle Raiders 26-0 in Canberra
stories.why_it_matters: The Sydney Roosters shut out the Canberra Raiders 26-0 last night at GIO Stadium — a statement result. DCE (Daly Cherry-Evans) and Walker (Adam Keighran is likely referenced in the Big Hits piece) were reportedly standout performers. The Raiders were held scoreless, which is rare in NRL and a sign the Roosters' defence is firing on all cylinders heading toward finals contention.

stories.title: Fremantle belt North Melbourne in biggest loss of Clarkson's coaching career
stories.why_it_matters: Fremantle recorded a record thrashing of North Melbourne today in what ESPN called a historic result — and Nine.com.au reports it's the biggest loss of Chris Clarkson's coaching career, leaving him 'bitterly disappointed'. Clarkson, who won four flags at Hawthorn, is struggling in his rebuilding job at North. Fremantle continue their strong 2026 form and are building into genuine finals contenders.

stories.title: Mirra Andreeva books French Open final spot with win over Marta Kostyuk 6-1, 6-3
stories.why_it_matters: Russia's Mirra Andreeva is through to her first Grand Slam final after dismantling Marta Kostyuk 6-1, 6-3 in the French Open semi-final at Court Philippe-Chatrier in Paris on June 4. Andreeva, one of the youngest players in the draw, was dominant throughout. She'll play in the Roland Garros final with a first major title on the line — a historic moment for the 20-year-old.
